btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurable adoption readings available for the sector. The figure comes from firms answering whether they used AI in the past two weeks, so it captures active deployment rather than stated intent.

The most established and consequential AI application in real estate is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical sales data, with Zestimates updating multiple times per week. HouseCanary covers more than 136 million U.S. properties with AI-powered valuations, forecasts, and analytics, applying machine learning and image recognition to assess property condition from photos. Opendoor uses pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, meaning its valuation AI carries real balance-sheet exposure rather than serving only as an informational tool.

Automated valuation models used in mortgage decisions are now federally regulated. The OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, NCUA, CFPB, and FHFA jointly adopted a final rule implementing quality control standards mandated by the Dodd-Frank Act, requiring institutions that use AVMs in credit decisions or securitization determinations to maintain policies and control systems ensuring high confidence in estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing. Per the CFPB, the rule applies to mortgage originators and secondary market issuers valuing collateral on a consumer's principal dwelling, making this the first binding federal framework specifically governing the sector's core AI.

Beyond valuation, AI is moving into day-to-day operations across both residential and commercial real estate. EliseAI deploys conversational and agentic AI for property management, handling leasing inquiries, scheduling tours, following up with prospects, and processing maintenance requests around the clock. Prophia applies document AI to commercial lease abstraction, extracting key terms and rent roll data from leases and combining AI output with expert validation to produce structured portfolio data. Building Engines offers an AI-powered property management platform called Prism, positioned as a JLL company, that uses the data already held by commercial property teams to automate recommendations and reduce operating costs. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics.

The proptech capital and conference ecosystem provides a rough gauge of where industry attention concentrates. CRETI maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies. CREtech convenes what it describes as the world's premier real estate AI conference, drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, with sessions led by operators actively deploying AI across portfolios. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures, functions as the residential side's technology accelerator, vetting and scaling tools aimed at agents and brokerages. Compass integrates AI into its brokerage platform for agent workflows and client services, and Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models that support virtual touring, portfolio management, and construction coordination.

A reader evaluating deployment should note that the sector has clear, production-grade AI in two clusters: valuation models with publicly documented methodologies and, increasingly, regulatory obligations, and operational automation covering leasing communications, lease abstraction, and building management. The regulatory environment for valuation AI is no longer speculative, as the interagency AVM rule establishes enforceable quality control, bias-avoidance, and testing requirements for any institution using these models in mortgage decisions. Outside that regulated perimeter, adoption is active but the evidence on ROI from the available sources is largely qualitative, centered on cost reduction, faster response times, and NOI improvement rather than audited figures, so organizations should weigh vendor claims against their own operational baselines before committing.
